section.heading: 4.2 Null Spaces, Column Spaces, Row Spaces, and Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: In applications of linear algebra, subspaces of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ usually arise in one of two ways: (1) as the set of all solutions to a system of homogeneous linear equations or (2) as the set of all linear combinations of certain specified vectors. In this section, we compare and contrast these two descriptions of subspaces, allowing us to practice using the concept of a subspace. Actually, as you will soon discover, we have been working with subspaces ever since Section 1.3. The main new feature here is the terminology. The section concludes with a discussion of the kernel and range of a linear transformation.
section.heading: The Null Space of a Matrix
section.paragraph: Consider the following system of homogeneous equations:
In matrix form, this system is written as $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ , where
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & - 2 \\ - 5 & 9 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Recall that the set of all $$\textbf{x}$$ that satisfy (1) is called the solution set of the system (1). Often it is convenient to relate this set directly to the matrix $$A$$ and the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ . We call the set of $$\textbf{x}$$ that satisfy $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ the null space of the matrix $$A$$ .

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The null space of an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , written as Nul $$A$$ , is the set of all solutions of the homogeneous equation $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ . In set notation,

section.paragraph: A more dynamic description of Nul $$A$$ is the set of all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ that are mapped into the zero vector of $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ via the linear transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ . See Figure 1.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be the matrix in (2), and let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 3 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Determine if $$\mathbf{u}$$ belongs to the null space of $$A$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: To test if $$\mathbf{u}$$ satisfies $$A\mathbf{u} = 0$$ , simply compute

$$A \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & - 2 \\ - 5 & 9 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & - & 9 & + & 4 \\ - 25 & + & 27 & - & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
Thus $$\mathbf{u}$$ is in Nul $$A$$ .

section.paragraph: The term space in null space is appropriate because the null space of a matrix is a vector space, as shown in the next theorem.

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: The null space of an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Equivalently, the set of all solutions to a system $$A\textbf{x} = 0$$ of $$m$$ homogeneous linear equations in $$n$$ unknowns is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Certainly Nul $$A$$ is a subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ because $$A$$ has $$n$$ columns. We must show that Nul $$A$$ satisfies the three properties of a subspace. Of course, $$0$$ is in Nul $$A$$ . Next, let $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\textbf{v}$$ represent any two vectors in Nul $$A$$ . Then
$$A \mathbf{u} = 0 \text{and} A \mathbf{v} = 0$$
To show that $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ is in Nul $$A$$ , we must show that $$A\left( {\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}} \right) = 0$$ . Using a property of matrix multiplication, compute
$$A \left(\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = A \mathbf{u} + A \mathbf{v} = 0 + 0 = 0$$
Thus $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ is in Nul $$A$$ , and Nul $$A$$ is closed under vector addition. Finally, if $$c$$ is any scalar, then
$$A \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} \left.\right) = c \left(\right. A \mathbf{u} \left.\right) = c \left(\right. 0 \left.\right) = 0$$
which shows that $$c\mathbf{u}$$ is in Nul $$A$$ . Thus Nul $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$H$$ be the set of all vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ whose coordinates $$a$$ , $$b$$ , $$c$$ , $$d$$ satisfy the equations $$a - 2b + 5c = d$$ and $$c - a = b$$ . Show that $$H$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Rearrange the equations that describe the elements of $$H$$ , and note that $$H$$ is the set of all solutions of the following system of homogeneous linear equations:
By Theorem 2, $$H$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ .

section.paragraph: It is important that the linear equations defining the set $$H$$ are homogeneous. Otherwise, the set of solutions will definitely not be a subspace (because the zero vector is not a solution of a nonhomogeneous system). Also, in some cases, the set of solutions could be empty.
section.heading: An Explicit Description of Nul A
section.paragraph: There is no obvious relation between vectors in Null $$A$$ and the entries in $$A$$ . We say that Nul $$A$$ is defined implicitly, because it is defined by a condition that must be checked. No explicit list or description of the elements in Nul $$A$$ is given. However, solving the equation $$A\textbf{x} = 0$$ amounts to producing an explicit description of Nul $$A$$ . The next example reviews the procedure from Section 1.5.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find a spanning set for the null space of the matrix
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The first step is to find the general solution of $$A\textbf{x} = 0$$ in terms of free variables. Row reduce the augmented matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} A & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ to reduced echelon form in order to write the basic variables in terms of the free variables:

The general solution is $$x_{1} = 2x_{2} + x_{4} - 3x_{5}$$ , $$x_{3} = - 2x_{4} + 2x_{5}$$ , with $$x_{2}$$ , $$x_{4}$$ , and $$x_{5}$$ free. Next, decompose the vector giving the general solution into a linear combination of vectors where the weights are the free variables. That is,

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \\ x_{4} \\ x_{5}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 x_{2} + x_{4} - 3 x_{5} \\ x_{2} \\ - 2 x_{4} + 2 x_{5} \\ x_{4} \\ x_{5}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = x_{2 } \underset{\begin{matrix}\uparrow \\ \textbf{u}\end{matrix}}{ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.} + x_{4 } \underset{\begin{matrix}\uparrow \\ \textbf{v}\end{matrix}}{ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0 \\ - 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.} + x_{5} \underset{\begin{matrix}\uparrow \\ \textbf{w}\end{matrix}}{ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.} & = x_{2} \textbf{u} + x_{4} \textbf{v} + x_{5} \textbf{w}$$

Every linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\textbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{w}$$ is an element of Nul $$A$$ and vice versa. Thus $$\left\{ \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w} \right\}$$ is a spanning set for Nul $$A$$ .

section.paragraph: Two points should be made about the solution of Example 3 that apply to all problems of this type where Nul $$A$$ contains nonzero vectors. We will use these facts later.

list.item: The spanning set produced by the method in Example 3 is automatically linearly independent because the free variables are the weights on the spanning vectors. For instance, look at the 2nd, 4th, and 5th entries in the solution vector in (3) and note that $$x_{2}\mathbf{u} + x_{4}\mathbf{v} + x_{5}\mathbf{w}$$ can be $$0$$ only if the weights $$x_{2} \text{,} x_{4}$$ , and $$x_{5}$$ are all zero.
When Nul $$A$$ contains nonzero vectors, the number of vectors in the spanning set for Nul $$A$$ equals the number of free variables in the equation $$A\textbf{x} = 0$$ .

section.heading: The Column Space of a Matrix
section.paragraph: Another important subspace associated with a matrix is its column space. Unlike the null space, the column space is defined explicitly via linear combinations.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The column space of an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , written as Col $$A$$ , is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $$A$$ . If $$A = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{a}_{1} & \ldots & \mathbf{a}_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$ , then

section.paragraph: Since $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{a}_{1}, \text{…} ,\mathbf{a}_{n} \right\}$$ is a subspace, by Theorem 1, the next theorem follows from the definition of Col $$A$$ and the fact that the columns of $$A$$ are in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ .

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: The column space of an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ .

section.paragraph: Note that a typical vector in Col $$A$$ can be written as $$A\mathbf{x}$$ for some $$\textbf{x}$$ because the notation $$A\textbf{x}$$ stands for a linear combination of the columns of $$A$$ . That is,
$$\boxed{ \text{Col} A = { \textbf{b} : \textbf{b} = \textit{A} \textbf{x} \text{for} \text{some} \textbf{x} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{n} }}$$

The notation $$A\textbf{x}$$ for vectors in Col $$A$$ also shows that Col $$A$$ is the range of the linear transformation $$\left. \textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x} \right.$$ . We will return to this point of view at the end of the section.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find a matrix $$A$$ such that $$W = \text{Col} A$$ .
$$W = \left{\right. \left[\right. 6 a - b a + b - 7 a \left]\right. : a , b in \mathbb{R} \left.\right}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, write $$W$$ as a set of linear combinations.

$$W = \left{\right. a \left[\right. 6 1 - 7 \left]\right. + b \left[\right. - 1 1 0 \left]\right. : a , b in \mathbb{R} \left.\right} = \text{Span} \left{\right. \left[\right. 6 1 - 7 \left]\right. , \left[\right. - 1 1 0 \left]\right. \left.\right}$$

image.alt: A figure shows a rectangular plane labeled W on a three-dimensional coordinate plane.

example.paragraph: Second, use the vectors in the spanning set as the columns of $$A$$ . Let $$A = \left[\right. 6 & - 1 1 & 1 - 7 & 0 \left]\right. .$$
Then $$W = \text{Col} A$$ , as desired.

section.paragraph: Recall from Theorem 4 in Section 1.4 that the columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ if and only if the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ . We can restate this fact as follows:

note.paragraph: The column space of an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ if and only if the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a solution for each $$\textbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ .

section.heading: The Row Space
section.paragraph: If $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix, each row of $$A$$ has $$n$$ entries and thus can be identified with a vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . The set of all linear combinations of the row vectors is called the row space of $$A$$ and is denoted by Row $$A$$ . Each row has $$n$$ entries, so Row $$A$$ is a subspace of $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Since the rows of $$A$$ are identified with the columns of $$A^{T}$$ , we could also write $$\text{Col} A^{T}$$ in place of Row $$A$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let

$$A = \left[\right. - 2 & - 5 & 8 & 0 & - 17 1 & 3 & - 5 & 1 & 5 3 & 11 & - 19 & 7 & 1 1 & 7 & - 13 & 5 & - 3 \left]\right. and \textbf{r}_{1} = \left(\right. - 2 , - 5 , 8 , 0 , - 17 \left.\right) \textbf{r}_{2} = \left(\right. 1 , 3 , - 5 , 1 , 5 \left.\right) \textbf{r}_{3} = \left(\right. 3 , 11 , - 19 , 7 , 1 \left.\right) \textbf{r}_{4} = \left(\right. 1 , 7 , - 13 , 5 , - 3 \left.\right)$$

The row space of $$A$$ is the subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ spanned by $$\left\{ \mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2},\mathbf{r}_{3},\mathbf{r}_{4} \right\}$$ . That is, Row $$A = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{r}_{1},\mathbf{r}_{2},\mathbf{r}_{3},\mathbf{r}_{4} \right\}$$ . It is natural to write row vectors horizontally; however, they may also be written as column vectors if that is more convenient.

section.heading: The Contrast Between Nul A and Col A
section.paragraph: It is natural to wonder how the null space and column space of a matrix are related. In fact, the two spaces are quite dissimilar, as Examples 6–8 will show. Nevertheless, a surprising connection between the null space and column space will emerge in Section 4.5, after more theory is available.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Let

list.item: If the column space of $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{k}$$ , what is $$k$$ ?
If the null space of $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{k}$$ , what is $$k$$ ?

example.heading: Solution

list.item: The columns of $$A$$ each have three entries, so Col $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{k}$$ , where $$k = 3$$ .
A vector $$\textbf{x}$$ such that $$A\textbf{x}$$ is defined must have four entries, so Nul $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{k}$$ , where $$k = 4$$ .

section.paragraph: When a matrix is not square, as in Example 6, the vectors in Nul $$A$$ and Col $$A$$ live in entirely different “universes.” For example, no linear combination of vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ can produce a vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ . When $$A$$ is square, Nul $$A$$ and Col $$A$$ do have the zero vector in common, and in special cases it is possible that some nonzero vectors belong to both Nul $$A$$ and Col $$A$$ .

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: With $$A$$ as in Example 6, find a nonzero vector in Col $$A$$ and a nonzero vector in Nul $$A$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: It is easy to find a vector in Col $$A$$ . Any column of $$A$$ will do, say, $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 2} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack.$$ To find a nonzero vector in Nul $$A$$ , row reduce the augmented matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} A & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and obtain
$$\left[\right. A & 0 \left]\right. ∼ \left[\right. 1 & 0 & 9 & 0 & 0 0 & 1 & - 5 & 0 & 0 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \left]\right.$$

Thus, if $$\textbf{x}$$ satisfies $$A\textbf{x} = 0$$ , then $$x_{1} = - 9x_{3}$$ , $$x_{2} = 5x_{3}$$ , $$x_{4} = 0$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ is free. Assigning a nonzero value to $$x_{3}$$ —say, $$x_{3} = 1$$ —we obtain a vector in Nul $$A$$ , namely, $$\mathbf{x} = ( - 9 \text{,} 5 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 0)$$ .

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: With $$A$$ as in Example 6, let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 1} \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

list.item: Determine if $$\mathbf{u}$$ is in Nul $$A$$ . Could $$\mathbf{u}$$ be in Col $$A$$ ?
Determine if $$\textbf{v}$$ is in Col $$A$$ . Could $$\textbf{v}$$ be in Nul $$A$$ ?

example.heading: Solution

list.item: An explicit description of Nul $$A$$ is not needed here. Simply compute the product $$A\textbf{u}$$ . $$A \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & - 2 & 1 \\ - 2 & - 5 & 7 & 3 \\ 3 & 7 & - 8 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ - 2 \\ - 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ - 3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ Obviously, $$\mathbf{u}$$ is not a solution of $$A\textbf{x} = 0$$ , so $$\mathbf{u}$$ is not in Nul $$A$$ . Also, with four entries, $$\mathbf{u}$$ could not possibly be in Col $$A$$ , since Col $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ .

Reduce $$\begin{bmatrix} A & \textbf{v} \end{bmatrix}$$ to an echelon form. $$\begin{bmatrix} A & \mathbf{v} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & - 2 & 1 & 3 \\ - 2 & - 5 & 7 & 3 & - 1 \\ 3 & 7 & - 8 & 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} ∼ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & - 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & - 5 & - 14 & - 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 17 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ At this point, it is clear that the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{v}$$ is consistent, so $$\textbf{v}$$ is in Col $$A$$ . With only three entries, $$\textbf{v}$$ could not possibly be in Nul $$A$$ , since Nul $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ .

section.paragraph: The table below summarizes what we have learned about Nul $$A$$ and Col $$A$$ . Item $$8$$ is a restatement of Theorems 11 and 12(a) in Section 1.9.
section.heading: Kernel and Range of a Linear Transformation
section.paragraph: Subspaces of vector spaces other than $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ are often described in terms of a linear transformation instead of a matrix. To make this precise, we generalize the definition given in Section 1.8.

image.alt: A table shows the difference between Nul A and Col A.

figure.caption: Contrast Between Nul A and Col A for an m×n Matrix A

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A linear transformation $$T$$ from a vector space $$V$$ into a vector space $$W$$ is a rule that assigns to each vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ a unique vector $$T\left( \textbf{x} \right)$$ in $$W$$ , such that

list.item: (i)﻿ $$T\left( \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \right) = T\left( \mathbf{u} \right) + T\left( \mathbf{v} \right)$$ for all $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$V$$ , and﻿
(ii)﻿ $$T\left( c\mathbf{u} \right) = cT\left( \mathbf{u} \right)$$ for all $$\mathbf{u}$$ in $$V$$ and all scalars $$c$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The kernel or null space) of such a $$T$$ is the set of all $$\mathbf{u}$$ in $$V$$ such that $$T(\mathbf{u}) = 0$$ (the zero vector in $$W$$ ). The range of $$T$$ is the set of all vectors in $$W$$ of the form $$T\left( \textbf{x} \right)$$ for some $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ . If $$T$$ happens to arise as a matrix transformation—say, $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ for some matrix $$A$$ —then the kernel and the range of $$T$$ are just the null space and the column space of $$A$$ , as defined earlier.

It is not difficult to show that the kernel of $$T$$ is a subspace of $$V$$ . The proof is essentially the same as the one for Theorem 2. Also, the range of $$T$$ is a subspace of $$W$$ . See Figure 2 and Exercise 42.

image.alt: A figure shows two planes labeled V and W facing each other.

figure.caption: Figure 2 Subspaces associated with a linear transformation

section.paragraph: In applications, a subspace usually arises as either the kernel or the range of an appropriate linear transformation. For instance, the set of all solutions of a homogeneous linear differential equation turns out to be the kernel of a linear transformation. Typically, such a linear transformation is described in terms of one or more derivatives of a function. To explain this in any detail would take us too far afield at this point. So we consider only two examples. The first explains why the operation of differentiation is a linear transformation.

example.heading: Example 9
(Calculus required)
example.paragraph: Let $$V$$ be the vector space of all real-valued functions $$f$$ defined on an interval $$\lbrack a \text{,} b\rbrack$$ with the property that they are differentiable and their derivatives are continuous functions on $$\lbrack a \text{,} b\rbrack$$ . Let $$W$$ be the vector space $$C\lbrack a \text{,} b\rbrack$$ of all continuous functions on $$\lbrack a \text{,} b\rbrack$$ , and let $$\left. D:V\rightarrow W \right.$$ be the transformation that changes $$f$$ in $$V$$ into its derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ . In calculus, two simple differentiation rules are
$$D \left(\right. f + g \left.\right) = D \left(\right. f \left.\right) + D \left(\right. g \left.\right) \text{and} D \left(\right. c f \left.\right) = c D \left(\right. f \left.\right)$$

That is, $$D$$ is a linear transformation. It can be shown that the kernel of $$D$$ is the set of constant functions on $$\lbrack a \text{,} b\rbrack$$ and the range of $$D$$ is the set $$W$$ of all continuous functions on $$\lbrack a \text{,} b\rbrack$$ .

The set of solutions of (4) is precisely the kernel of the linear transformation that maps a function $$y = f(t)$$ into the function $$f''(t) + \omega^{2}f(t)$$ . Finding an explicit description of this vector space is a problem in differential equations. The solution set turns out to be the space described in Exercise 19 in Section 4.1.

section.paragraph: A common technique used in the stock market is technical analysis. Statistical trends gathered from stock-trading activity, such as price movement and volume, are analyzed. Technical analysts focus on patterns of stock-price movements, trading signals, and various other analytical charting tools to evaluate a security’s strength or weakness. A moving average is a commonly used indicator in technical analysis. It smooths out price action by filtering out the effects from random price fluctuations. In the final example for this section, we examine the linear transformation that creates the two-day moving average from a “signal” of daily prices. We will look at moving average transformations that average over a longer period of time in Section 4.7.

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Let $$\{ p_{k}\}$$ in $$\text{S}$$ represent the price of a stock that has been recorded daily over an extended period of time. Note that we can assume that $$p_{k} = 0$$ for $$k$$ outside the time period under study. To create a two-day moving average, the mapping $$\left. M_{2}:\mathbb{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{S} \right.$$ defined by $$M_{2}\left( \left\{ p_{k} \right\} \right) = \left\{ \frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2} \right\}$$ is applied to the data. Show that $$M_{2}$$ is a linear transformation and find its kernel.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: To see that $$M_{2}$$ is a linear transformation, observe that for two signals $$\{ p_{k}\}$$ and $$\{ q_{k}\}$$ in $$\text{S}$$ and any scalar $$c$$ ,

$$M_{2} \left(\right. \left{\right. p_{k} \left.\right} + \left{\right. q_{k} \left.\right} \left.\right) = M_{2} \left(\right. \left{\right. p_{k} + q_{k} \left.\right} \left.\right) & = & \left{\frac{p_{k} + q_{k} + p_{k - 1} + q_{k - 1}}{2}\right} & = & \left{\frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2}\right} + \left{\frac{q_{k} + q_{k - 1}}{2}\right} & = & M_{2} \left(\left{p_{k}\right}\right) + M_{2} \left(\left{q_{k}\right}\right)$$
and

$$M_{2} \left(\right. c \left{\right. p_{k} \left.\right} \left.\right) = M_{2} \left(\right. \left{\right. c p_{k} \left.\right} \left.\right) = \left{\frac{c p_{k} + c p_{k - 1}}{2}\right} = c \left{\frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2}\right} = c M_{2} \left(\right. \left{\right. p_{k} \left.\right} \left.\right)$$
thus $$M_{2}$$ is a linear transformation.

To find the kernel of $$M_{2}$$ , notice that $$\left\{ p_{k} \right\}$$ is in the kernel if and only if $$\frac{p_{k} + p_{k - 1}}{2} = 0$$ for all $$k$$ , and hence $$p_{k} = - p_{k - 1}$$ . Since this relationship is true for all integers $$k$$ , it can be applied recursively resulting in $$p_{k} = - p_{k - 1} = \left( {- 1} \right)^{2}p_{k - 2} = \left( {- 1} \right)^{3}p_{k - 3}\ldots$$ . Working out from $$k = 0$$ , any signal in the kernel can be written as $$p_{k} = p_{0}\left( {- 1} \right)^{k}$$ , a multiple of the alternating signal described by $$\left\{ \left( {- 1} \right)^{k} \right\}$$ . Since the kernel of the two-day moving average function consists of all multiples of the alternating sequence, it smooths out daily fluctuations, without leveling out overall trends. (See Figure 3.)

image.alt: A graph shows two lines that depict the original signal and the moving average.

list.item: Let $$W = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}:a - 3b - c = 0 \right\}$$ . Show in two different ways that $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . (Use two theorems.)

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & - 3 & 5 \\ - 4 & 1 & - 5 \\ - 5 & 2 & - 4 \end{bmatrix} ,$$ $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ and $$\mathbf{w} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 6 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack.$$ Suppose you know that the equations $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{v}$$ and $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{w}$$ are both consistent. What can you say about the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{v} + \textbf{w}$$ ?
Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix. If $$\text{Col} A = \text{Nul} A,$$ show that Null $$A^{2} = \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .
